issues.legal_issue: A statutory religious-endowment board lacks jurisdiction to decide which claimant succeeds to an office whose hereditary character is undisputed.
material_facts: The office of trustee had been held hereditarily, and the parties accepted that it was a hereditary office.
The dispute was whether one family member or other competing family members were entitled to succeed to the deceased trustee.
The claimant asked the Board to declare him the successor, and the Board decided that claim in his favour.
issues.conclusion: The dispute was not one the Board could decide under Section 84(1)(b); jurisdiction to determine the competing claims to succession lay with the ordinary civil courts. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court decision and restored the District Judge’s order setting aside the Board’s decision.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 84(1)(b) and 9(6) of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1926, concern whether a trustee holds office as a hereditary trustee, not which person is entitled to succeed to an office accepted to be hereditary. The definition of trustee in Section 9(13) and the distinction between hereditary and non-hereditary trustees support that reading. The Court applied the principle in Sastri Ammal v. Prayalavarna Naicker and A. Krishnaswami Raja v. Krishna Raja, which construed the analogous Section 57(b) of the 1951 Act as not authorising determination of competing succession claims. Sections 84(2)–(4) provide for review of the Board’s decisions but do not enlarge the matters within its jurisdiction under subsection (1).

predicates.religious_endowment_board_proceeding: A dispute concerning the management of a religious endowment is brought before a statutory board for determination.
predicates.hereditary_status_undisputed: The parties accept that the office in question is hereditary.
predicates.dispute_concerns_successor_identity: The parties disagree about which claimant is entitled to succeed to the hereditary office.
predicates.board_lacks_jurisdiction_to_decide_succe: The board has no authority to decide which claimant succeeds to the hereditary office.

issues.definition: When a religious-endowment board is asked to resolve a dispute over who succeeds to an office whose hereditary status is undisputed, it cannot decide that successor claim.

issues.legal_issue: A party that obtains dismissal of a board proceeding on the basis that the hereditary character of the office is undisputed cannot later retract that position in other proceedings.
material_facts: In challenging the Board’s jurisdiction, a contestant accepted for the dispute that the office was hereditary.
The Supreme Court dismissed the Board’s decision as beyond its jurisdiction because the dispute concerned succession to an office whose hereditary character was not disputed.
issues.conclusion: The contestant could not resile in other proceedings from the position that the hereditary character of the office was undisputed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court stated that a contestant who had obtained dismissal of the proceedings as without jurisdiction on the ground that no dispute about the hereditary nature of the office arose could not later resile from that position. The Court cited no separate statutory provision or earlier case for this point.

predicates.board_jurisdiction_challenge: A party challenges a board’s authority to decide a dispute concerning a religious-endowment office.
predicates.party_asserted_no_dispute_over_hereditar: A party maintains that the office’s hereditary character is undisputed and relies on that position to obtain dismissal of the board proceeding.
predicates.party_cannot_retract_that_position_in_la: The party cannot later take the contrary position about whether the office is hereditary.

issues.definition: A party that obtains dismissal of a board proceeding by maintaining that the office’s hereditary character is undisputed cannot later take the contrary position.
